summary: This unit teaches you to order the materials a job needs: the right items, in the right amounts, from a good supplier, in time. You will learn to work out quantities from a drawing or cutting list, describe items fully, check the store first, use simple stock control, compare suppliers, complete a requisition and purchase order, receive and check deliveries, deal with problems, store materials safely, and keep the paperwork that links it all together.

blocks.p: Every job, whether it is a steel gate or the wiring of a shop, needs materials: steel, cable, fittings, fixings and consumables such as electrodes, grinding discs and paint. If the wrong item arrives, or too little, or it arrives late, the job stops and money is lost. If far too much is bought, money sits on the shelf and stock spoils. This unit teaches you to order materials **accurately, on time and at the best value**.

**Who it is for:** trainees in Welding and Fabrication and in Electrical Installation at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other training centres, and anyone who orders, receives or stores materials in a workshop or on site. The examples come from both trades.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Read the drawing, job sheet or cutting list; list every item with its quantity, including fixings and consumables; change quantities into the units the supplier sells.
Give the type, size, grade or rating, finish and quantity, so the right item arrives first time.
See what is already in the store or on site, use the stock records, and order only what is needed.
Use the approved supplier list, get prices for the same items, and compare quality, delivery time and total cost to find the best value.
Complete a purchase requisition, get it approved, complete the purchase order, place the order and confirm it in writing.
Check the goods against the purchase order and delivery note before signing, and record what actually arrived.
Record shortages, damage and wrong items, keep them apart, and report them so they are put right.
Store each material safely and in good condition, and lift and move it safely.
Link the requisition, order, delivery note, goods received note, invoice and credit note, and file them.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on working out quantities, describing materials, stock control, suppliers, orders, deliveries, storage, handling and paperwork.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as quantity, each, buffer stock, back order, stocktake, credit note; and simple sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: preparing a materials list, requisition and purchase order for a job, including a phone order role play; and receiving, checking and storing a delivery that has mistakes in it, then updating the stock records.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator to class and practise the sums in this kit until they are quick. In the exam and at work, always round **up** to whole packs, lengths or rolls.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Start from the job's documents, never from memory or from what was ordered last time. Each job is different.

head: Document
What it gives you
rows: The parts, their sizes and the materials; on electrical drawings, the outlets, switches, lights and circuits
The materials, finishes and standards the customer wants, and the date the job starts
Every piece of steel to be cut: section, size, length and how many
Bill of materials or materials list
Every item to be bought or drawn from the store, with quantities

flow: Read the drawing, job sheet and cutting list, including the notes
List every item: main materials, **fixings** (bolts, screws, anchors, hinges, clips) and **consumables** (electrodes, discs, paint, cable ties, tape)
Give each item a full description and work out the quantity
Change the quantities into the units the supplier sells (lengths, rolls, boxes, sheets, tins) and **round up**
Add a small allowance for cutting and waste
Check the store and the site, and take away what you already have
Note the date each item is needed, so the order goes in early enough
Have the list checked by your supervisor

blocks.p: Steel bar, tube and sections are sold in **stock lengths** (often 6 m, about 20 ft). Do not just add up the lengths: plan how the pieces come out of each length, allowing for the saw cut (the **kerf**, often 2–3 mm on a bandsaw or abrasive saw). A piece cannot be made from two offcuts.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: A gate needs 4 pieces of 1800 mm and 2 pieces of 1200 mm of square tube. Tube comes in 6 m lengths.
Total length = 4 × 1.8 + 2 × 1.2 = 9.6 m, which looks like 2 lengths
Length 1: 1800 + 1800 + 1800 = 5400 mm + 3 cuts; about 590 mm left over (too short for another piece)
Length 2: 1800 + 1200 + 1200 = 4200 mm + 3 cuts; about 1790 mm left over
Answer: **2 lengths**, with a useful offcut
The same gate, but with 5 uprights of 2100 mm.
Total = 10.5 m, which looks like 2 lengths
Each 6 m length gives only 2 pieces of 2100 mm (4200 mm), leaving 1800 mm, too short for a third

head: Worked example
Working
rows: Bolts come in boxes of 50. You need 135.
135 ÷ 50 = 2.7, so **3 boxes**. Never order 2.7 boxes, and never round down.
PVC conduit comes in 3 m lengths. The runs add up to 46 m, plus 10% for offcuts and bends.
Cable comes in 100 m rolls. Three circuits need 32 m, 38 m and 45 m of the same cable.
32 + 38 + 45 = 115 m, so **2 rolls** (and check whether each circuit needs more than one conductor of that cable)
Electrodes cost J$3,950 a 5 kg packet. You need 4 packets.

blocks.note: Always check your sums a second way, for example by estimating first (4 packets at about J$4,000 is about J$16,000). A slip of one zero can order ten times too much.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Ordering too much or too little

head: Too much
Too little
rows: Money tied up in stock that may not be used
Stock that rusts, gets damp, dries out or goes out of date
Store space filled and harder to manage
Work stops while you wait for more
Extra delivery charges and time spent ordering again
The job finishes late and the customer is unhappy

blocks.p: A small, planned allowance for waste is good practice. A large, unplanned 'just in case' extra is waste.

A supplier sells hundreds of sizes and types of each item. An order such as "some angle iron" or "cable" invites the wrong goods, and wrong goods mean delay, return trips, extra cost, and sometimes an unsafe job. Describe each item so that **nobody could deliver the wrong thing**.

ul: **What it is:** the type of item or section (flat bar, angle, plate, socket outlet, circuit breaker).
**Size:** every dimension that matters, in the units the supplier uses.
**Grade, rating or standard:** mild steel, galvanised; current and voltage rating; cable type.
**Finish or colour** where it matters: black (bare) steel, galvanised, primed; insulation colour.
**Length or pack size:** 6 m lengths, 1220 × 2440 mm sheets, 100 m rolls, boxes of 50.
**Quantity**, in those units.

head: Item
How it is described
Example
rows: 40 × 6 mm mild steel flat bar, 6 m lengths, qty 4
50 × 50 × 5 mm mild steel angle, 6 m lengths, qty 6
Square or rectangular hollow section (SHS, RHS)
50 × 50 × 2.0 mm mild steel SHS, 6 m lengths, qty 3
Outside diameter (or nominal bore) × wall thickness, length, finish
25 mm (1 in) galvanised (GI) pipe, wall or weight as specified, 6 m lengths, qty 2
12 mm mild steel round bar, 6 m lengths, qty 10
3 mm mild steel sheet, 1220 × 2440 mm, qty 2

blocks.note: Many Jamaican suppliers still describe steel in inches and feet, for example "1½ in × ¼ in flat bar, 20 ft lengths" or "4 × 8 ft sheet". 1 inch = 25.4 mm and 1 foot = 304.8 mm, so a 4 × 8 ft sheet is about 1220 × 2440 mm and a 20 ft length is about 6.1 m. Check which units the price list uses, and write the size the way the supplier will understand it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Item
Details to give
Example
rows: Type, conductor size, number of cores, insulation colour, length or roll size
12 AWG THHN copper wire, black, 500 ft (about 152 m) roll, qty 2
Type (single or duplex), current and voltage rating, colour
Duplex socket outlet, 20 A 125 V, white, qty 26
Type to suit the panel, number of poles, current rating
Single-pole 20 A breaker for the panel make in use, qty 3
Material (PVC or steel), size, length; type of fitting
20 mm PVC conduit, 3 m lengths, qty 17
Type, lamp type and wattage, voltage
LED batten 1.2 m, 36 W, 110–240 V, qty 8

blocks.note: Wire and cable sizes in Jamaica are often given in **AWG** (American Wire Gauge, where a **smaller** number means a **thicker** wire), and lengths are sometimes priced by the foot. Copy sizes exactly from the drawing or specification: a smaller wire or a lower-rated fitting than the design asks for is unsafe.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Electrodes: type, diameter and pack weight, for example E6013, 3.2 mm, 5 kg packets.
Grinding and cutting discs: type (grinding, cutting or flap), diameter, thickness, bore, and maximum speed rating to suit the grinder, for example 115 mm cutting disc for steel, 1 mm thick.
Paint: type (primer, enamel), colour, tin size in litres.
Fixings: type, diameter, length, finish, pack size, for example M10 × 40 mm galvanised hex bolts with nuts and washers, box of 50.

head: Unit
Symbol or short form
Used for
rows: Sizes and lengths of steel, conduit and cable
Area of sheet materials, mesh, paint coverage
Electrodes and filler wire (sold by weight); steel bought in bulk
Single items: a hinge, a breaker, a light fitting

blocks.h: Common short forms on orders and price lists

head: Short form
Meaning
rows: Galvanised iron (zinc-coated steel), as in GI pipe or GI sheet
Back order: not in stock now; will be sent later

blocks.p: For structural or pressure work the specification may ask for a particular steel grade, and the supplier may provide a **test certificate** (mill certificate) that proves the steel's grade and strength. Ask for it when the job specification needs it, and keep it with the job records.

sections.title: Checking stock and simple stock control

blocks.p: Before ordering, look at what is already in the store and on site. Ordering what you already have wastes money and space. A simple **stock control** system tells you what you have, when to reorder and how much.

A **bin card** (stock card) is kept for each item, on the shelf or in a computer. Every time stock comes in or goes out, it is written down with the new balance, so anyone can see how much there should be.
Each new balance = the last balance + what came in − what went out. Check: 25 − 6 = 19; 19 + 20 = 39; 39 − 9 = 30.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The time from placing an order to the goods arriving
Extra stock kept in case a delivery is late or use is higher than usual
The balance at which a new order must be placed, so the new stock arrives before the buffer is used up
How much is ordered each time
The most that should be held, so money and space are not wasted
The oldest stock is issued first, so nothing sits until it spoils or goes out of date
Counting everything in the store and comparing the count with the records

blocks.p: **Reorder level = usage per day × lead time in days + buffer stock**

head: Worked example
Working
rows: A shop uses about 4 grinding discs a working day. The supplier takes 3 working days to deliver. The shop keeps a buffer of 10 discs.
Use during the lead time = 4 × 3 = 12 discs
When the balance falls to 22, order more: the 12 used while waiting leave the 10 in the buffer

ul: Put new deliveries **behind or under** the older stock, so the older stock is picked first.
Write the date received on packets, tins and boxes.
Check use-by dates on items such as paint, sealants, adhesives and some electrodes.
Report stock that is damaged, damp or out of date; do not issue it.
Count every item and compare the count with the bin card or computer record.
Where they differ, count again; then report the difference to the person in charge. It may be a recording mistake, an unrecorded issue, damage or theft.
The records are corrected only with the supervisor's approval, and the reason is noted.
Regular stocktakes keep the records right, so reorder levels work.

blocks.note: Never take stock without recording it, even one disc or a few metres of cable 'for a quick job'. Unrecorded issues make the records wrong, and the store runs out when the card says there is plenty. If you see stock running low, tell the person in charge of ordering.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Most businesses and training centres keep a list of **approved suppliers**: suppliers that have been checked for reliable quality, delivery and fair dealing. Buy from the list unless your supervisor agrees otherwise. Never buy from a friend or a roadside seller just because it is cheap.

ul: Look up prices on the supplier's **price list** or catalogue, or ask for a **quotation** (a written price for the exact items, valid for a stated time).
Ask at least two or three approved suppliers to price **exactly the same items**, so the prices can be compared fairly.
Check what each price includes: delivery, cutting to length, and **General Consumption Tax (GCT)** at the current rate. Compare all prices on the same basis (all with GCT or all without).

blocks.h: Best value, not just the lowest price

head: Compare
Questions to ask
rows: Unit price × quantity, plus delivery and any extra charges; any discount for a larger order or quick payment?
Right grade, rating and standard? Approved and safe electrical fittings? Rust-free steel? Discs marked with their speed rating?
Do they have it now? Will it arrive before the job starts?
Can they deliver to the site, with long lengths, and when?
Cash, cheque or account? How many days to pay?
How did they handle past problems, returns and credit notes?

head: Worked example: 10 packets of E6013 3.2 mm electrodes (all prices before GCT)
Supplier A
Supplier B
Supplier C
rows: J$37,000 plus a trip to collect

blocks.p: Supplier C has the lowest price but cannot supply in time. A and B cost the same in total, but A delivers in 2 days. If the job starts in 5 days, **A is the best value**.

blocks.note: Choose the best value, write down why on the comparison sheet, and get your supervisor's approval. A clear record of the comparison protects you and the business.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Requisitions, purchase orders and placing the order

flow: Find that materials are needed (from the job, or stock at its reorder level)
Check the store and stock records first
Complete a **purchase requisition**: an internal request to buy, with full descriptions, quantities, job number and date needed
An **authorised person** (supervisor, manager or purchasing officer) checks and approves it
Choose the supplier (compare prices, as in the last section)
Complete the **purchase order** (PO), signed by an authorised person, and send it to the supplier
Get the supplier's **order confirmation**, check it, and file copies of everything

blocks.p: Approval controls spending: it stops wrong, duplicate or unauthorised orders, and makes sure there is money in the budget for the job.

blocks.h: What goes on a purchase order

head: Part
Example
rows: PO 0457 (the supplier quotes it on the delivery note and invoice)
As on the approved supplier list
Site address, access notes, contact name and phone number
Full description, quantity and unit (qty 6, 6 m lengths)
Total, and GCT shown as the business requires
Goods total, delivery, GCT at the current rate, order total
The person allowed to approve spending

ul: Send the PO by email, hand it in, or place the order by phone, as the business does.
If you order by phone, **confirm it in writing** (send the PO or an email), and write down the date, the name of the person you spoke to, and the order number.
Tell the supplier the delivery address, how to get there (for example narrow road, no truck access after 4 p.m.), and a contact name and phone number on site.
For long lengths and heavy items, say whether there is a forklift or crane on site, or whether the supplier's truck must have one.

blocks.p: The supplier often sends an **order confirmation** (acknowledgement). Check it line by line against your PO: items, sizes, quantities, prices, delivery date and address. If anything is wrong, contact the supplier **at once**, before the goods are sent, and confirm the correction in writing.

ul: Note the promised delivery date and check that it arrives. If it is late, contact the supplier and tell your supervisor, because the job may be held up.
If the supplier cannot send part of the order now, it is a **back order**: find out when it will come, and whether another approved supplier can fill the gap.
If the lead time is longer than the time before the job starts, tell your supervisor at once: find another approved supplier or move the start date. Never just hope it comes early.

sections.title: Receiving deliveries and dealing with problems

ul: Have the purchase order to hand.
Clear a safe, level unloading area near the store, with a clear route for carrying.
Have the right help and equipment ready: trolley, forklift with a trained driver, or enough people for long lengths.
Wear gloves and safety boots.

flow: Compare the **delivery note** with the **purchase order**: are they the same items and quantities?
Count every item
Check the sizes and descriptions: measure steel with a tape and check thickness with a **vernier caliper**; read the labels on cable, fittings and packets
Check the condition: bent or kinked lengths, heavy rust, wet or torn packets of electrodes, broken fittings, damaged cable drums
Only then sign the delivery note, writing any problems on it first

blocks.note: Your signature on the delivery note says the goods arrived **complete and in good condition**. Sign only what you have checked. If the driver cannot wait, write the problem or "not checked" on the note before signing, check at once, and report anything wrong the same day.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Write exactly what arrived on the delivery note, for example "8 lengths received, 10 ordered". Ask the driver to sign or note it too. Report it.
Write the damage on the note, take photos, keep the items apart and labelled, and do not use them. Report it.
Write "40 × 5 mm received; 40 × 6 mm ordered" (or similar) on the note. Do not use them; keep them apart and labelled for return.
Record what arrived and what is to follow, and tell your supervisor when the rest is due.

flow: Record the problem on the delivery note before signing, with photos
Keep wrong or damaged goods separate, labelled and safe
Tell your supervisor straight away: the job may be held up
Contact the supplier the same day, by phone and in writing, quoting the order number, and ask for the missing or correct items and collection of the wrong ones
Get a **credit note** for anything returned or not received, and file the papers together

blocks.p: After checking, complete a **goods received note (GRN)**. It is the business's own record of what actually arrived, in what condition, and who checked it. It is used to update the stock records and to check the supplier's invoice, so the business pays only for what it received.

head: GRN shows
Example
rows: 6 September, from the approved steel supplier
PO number and delivery note number
Each item: ordered, received, accepted, rejected
2 lengths bent; photos taken; supplier phoned 10:15 a.m.

ul: Goods sent back to the supplier because they are wrong or damaged are called **returns**.
A **credit note** from the supplier reduces what the business owes, for returned goods, shortages or an overcharge.
Keep the rejected goods until the supplier collects them or tells you what to do; get a signature when they are collected.

head: Material
How to store it
Why
rows: On strong horizontal racks, off the floor, under cover
Heavy items low; long ends not sticking out into walkways
Keeps it straight, dry and easy to find; stops trips and head injuries
Flat on bearers off the floor, or upright in a proper plate rack, secured
Galvanised sheets kept dry, with air between them
Stops bending, rust, and sheets sliding or falling
Dry and sealed in their packets, in a dry store, as the maker says
Opened low-hydrogen electrodes in an electrode oven
Damp electrodes give poor, porous welds
Upright and chained, in a ventilated, shaded place away from heat
Oxygen kept apart from fuel gases (a common rule is at least 6 m, or a fire-resistant wall between them)
Valves closed and caps on; full and empty cylinders apart
Stops falls, leaks feeding a fire, and heated cylinders bursting
Dry, off the floor, out of the sun
Drums on a stand or chocked so they cannot roll; cut ends sealed
Keeps insulation sound and the right cable easy to find
In labelled bins or boxes, sorted by type and rating
In their own labelled containers with lids tight
In a ventilated store away from sparks, heat and the welding area
Fire extinguisher nearby; never in drink bottles
They are flammable, and some vapours are harmful

blocks.note: Jamaica's sun and rain damage stock left outside: steel rusts, electrode packets soak up damp, cable insulation cracks in strong sunlight, and cylinders heat up. Store everything under cover, and never leave a delivery sitting in the yard overnight.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Plan the move: check the weight and length, clear the route and the place where it will go, and check the ground is firm and dry.
Wear gloves (sharp edges and burrs) and safety boots (dropped loads).
Use a trolley, forklift or hoist for heavy loads. Forklifts and cranes are used **only by trained, authorised people**.
When lifting by hand: feet apart, bend your knees, keep your back straight, hold the load close, lift smoothly and do not twist. Get help for anything too heavy or awkward.
Carry long lengths with **two people, one at each end**, talking to each other, moving together, and taking care at corners and doorways.
Roll cable drums only in the direction of the arrow on the drum, or lift them with a drum stand or spindle.
Never throw materials off a truck, never stand under a raised load, and never climb racks.

blocks.h: PPE in the store and when unloading

head: Task
PPE
rows: Unloading and carrying steel and sheet
Leather gloves, safety boots; hard hat where loads are lifted overhead
Gloves suited to the chemical, safety glasses; follow the label

blocks.p: Each document in an order has a job, and they link together through the **order number**. Together they show what was asked for, what was ordered, what arrived and what must be paid.

head: Document
Who makes it
What it does
rows: You or the person who needs the goods
Internal request to buy; approved by an authorised person
The business (signed by an authorised person)
The order sent to the supplier, with its own number
Confirms what will be sent, at what price and when
Lists what the supplier says was sent; you sign it
Records what actually arrived and was accepted
Reduces what is owed, for returns, shortages or overcharges
Lists invoices, credit notes and payments, and what is still owed

blocks.p: Before an invoice is paid, it is matched with the **purchase order** (what was ordered, at what price) and the **goods received note** (what actually arrived). This is often called a three-way match. Pay only for what was ordered and received, at the agreed price. Query any difference with the supplier, and ask for a credit note where needed.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: The PO is for 4 sheets of 3 mm plate at J$18,500 each. The GRN shows 3 sheets received. The invoice charges for 4.
Query the invoice: ask for a credit note for J$18,500 (or a corrected invoice), or for the missing sheet to be delivered

ul: File all the papers for an order together, under the order number or job number.
Records let anyone trace an order if there is a problem, check what was paid, and see which suppliers deliver on time.
Keep records accurate and legible: date everything and sign where asked.
Keep copies of emails and notes of phone calls about the order.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can work out the materials a job needs from a drawing, job sheet or cutting list, including fixings and consumables.
I can plan cuts from stock lengths and change quantities into supplier units, always rounding up.
I can describe steel, electrical items and consumables fully, in the units the supplier uses.
I can check the store first and order only what is needed.
I can keep a bin card, work out a balance and a reorder level, and explain FIFO, buffer stock, lead time and stocktakes.
I can compare suppliers on total cost, quality and delivery time, and choose the best value.
I can complete a purchase requisition and a purchase order, and explain why they are approved.
I can place an order, confirm it in writing, and check the supplier's confirmation.
I can receive a delivery, check it against the purchase order and delivery note, and sign only when it is right.
I can record and report shortages, damage and wrong items, and complete a goods received note.
I can store steel, electrodes, gas cylinders, cable and paints safely.
I can lift and move materials safely, using help and equipment.
I can explain how the order documents link, and why an invoice is checked before it is paid.

terms: A supplier the business has checked and agreed to buy from
Part of an order the supplier cannot send now and will send later
A stock card showing stock in, stock out and the balance for one item
Extra stock kept in case a delivery is late; also called safety stock
A note from the supplier reducing what you owe
A list of every piece to be cut, with its section, size, length and number
The supplier's list of the goods sent, which comes with the delivery
First in, first out: the oldest stock is used first
General Consumption Tax, added to many prices in Jamaica at the current rate
The business's own record of what arrived and was accepted
The supplier's bill asking for payment
The width of material removed by a saw cut
The time from placing an order to delivery
The supplier's reply confirming the items, prices and delivery date
A supplier's list of items and their prices; also a catalogue
The numbered, signed document sent to a supplier to order goods
An internal request asking for materials to be bought
A supplier's written price for the exact items asked for
The stock balance at which more must be ordered
Goods sent back to the supplier because they are wrong or damaged
A supplier's summary of invoices, credits and payments, and what is owed
The length a bar or tube is sold in, often 6 m
Counting all the stock and comparing it with the records

c1.title: A driveway gate in Half Way Tree
c1.text: Alicia is a trainee at a small fabrication shop in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. Her supervisor, Mr Fraser, asks her to make the materials list for a driveway gate. The cutting list shows the frame and uprights in 50 × 50 × 2.0 mm mild steel square hollow section (SHS), which the supplier sells in 6 m lengths. The gate needs 5 uprights of 2100 mm. The drawing also shows two heavy hinges, a drop bolt, primer and gloss paint. The store rack has one 6 m length of SHS left over from another job.

c2.title: Wiring a variety shop in Santa Cruz
c2.text: Romario, an electrical installation trainee, is helping to order materials to wire a small variety shop in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. The drawing shows 26 duplex socket outlets. The supplier's price list gives socket outlets at J$650 each, or J$5,900 for a box of 10. The PVC conduit runs add up to 46 m, the conduit comes in 3 m lengths, and the supplier prices wire by the foot. Romario's supervisor wants about 10% extra conduit for offcuts and bends.

c3.title: The training centre store in Falmouth
c3.text: Nadine is helping Mrs Clarke, the storekeeper at a training centre in Falmouth, Trelawny. The bin card for 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes (5 kg packets) shows a balance of 18 packets on Monday morning. During the week 4 packets are issued on Monday, 5 on Tuesday, 10 are received on Wednesday, and 6 are issued on Thursday. The welding classes use about 3 packets a working day, the supplier delivers 4 working days after an order, and the Centre keeps a buffer of 5 packets.

c4.title: A steel delivery in Morant Bay
c4.text: Sheldon is the senior trainee on a site in Morant Bay, St Thomas, where his team is building steel roof trusses for a community centre. Purchase order PO 1128 was for 12 lengths of 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle, 6 lengths of 40 × 6 mm flat bar and 4 sheets of 3 mm plate. The truck arrives late in the afternoon, and the driver asks Sheldon to sign quickly so he can leave. Sheldon counts 12 lengths of angle, 2 of them badly bent; 6 lengths of flat bar that measure 5 mm thick with a vernier caliper; and 3 sheets of plate.

c5.title: Three prices for a shop in Bull Bay
c5.text: Damion works for a small welding shop in Bull Bay, St Andrew. He needs 20 grinding discs and 10 packets of electrodes for a job that starts in 4 days. Supplier A, on the approved list, quotes J$41,000 with free delivery in 2 days. Supplier B, also approved, quotes J$38,500 plus J$3,500 delivery, in 7 days. A friend of one of the welders offers the same items for J$34,000, cash only, with no receipt; his discs have no markings. Not every quote says whether GCT is included.

questions.q: How many 6 m lengths of SHS are needed for the 5 uprights of 2100 mm?
o: 2 lengths
3 lengths
4 lengths
5 lengths
questions.why: Each 6 m length gives only two 2100 mm pieces (4200 mm), and the 1800 mm left over is too short for a third. Five uprights need 2 + 2 + 1 pieces, so 3 lengths, even though they add up to only 10.5 m.

questions.q: Which line on Alicia's list describes the SHS fully?
o: 50 × 50 mm square hollow section, mild steel, qty 3
Mild steel square tube, 2.0 mm wall, 6 m lengths, qty 3
50 × 50 × 2.0 mm mild steel SHS, 6 m lengths, qty 3
50 × 50 × 2.0 mm square tube, 6 m lengths, black or GI
questions.why: A full description gives the section, every size (outside size and wall), the material or finish, the length it comes in and the quantity. Each of the other lines leaves out something the supplier needs.

questions.q: What should Alicia do about the 6 m length already in the store?
o: If it is sound and the right size, order one length fewer
Order the full amount anyway so there is a spare length in the rack
Leave it for the other job and order everything new
Use it for the uprights and order the frame in a smaller size
questions.why: Checking stock first stops money being spent on what the shop already has. She checks the stored length is the same section and in good condition, and records that it is taken for this job.

questions.q: Alicia's first list has only the steel on it. What else belongs on the list?
o: Nothing else, since the welders bring their own supplies
Only the paint, because the hinges come with the steel
Only the items that cost more than J$5,000 each
The hinges, drop bolt, paint, electrodes and discs
questions.why: A materials list includes the fittings, fixings and consumables as well as the main material. A job held up for want of a hinge or a box of electrodes costs as much as one held up for steel.

questions.q: Which is the cheapest way to buy the 26 socket outlets?
o: 3 full boxes of 10 outlets each
26 outlets bought singly
1 box and 16 single outlets
2 boxes and 6 single outlets
questions.why: Two boxes and six singles cost 2 × 5,900 + 6 × 650 = J$15,700. Three boxes cost J$17,700, 26 singles J$16,900, and one box with 16 singles J$16,300.

questions.q: How many 3 m lengths of conduit should Romario order, with the 10% extra?
o: 15 lengths
16 lengths
17 lengths
20 lengths
questions.why: 46 m plus 10% is 50.6 m, and 50.6 ÷ 3 = 16.9, which rounds up to 17 lengths. Sixteen lengths would cover the runs with no allowance, and fifteen would not even do that.

questions.q: Romario needs 150 m of one wire, and the supplier prices it by the foot. About how many feet should he ask for?
o: About 50 ft
About 150 ft
About 500 ft
About 1500 ft
questions.why: One foot is 0.3048 m, so 150 m ÷ 0.3048 is about 492 ft, which rounds up to about 500 ft. A metre is a little over 3 feet, so the number of feet is always a little over three times the number of metres.

questions.q: The order confirmation lists 25 mm conduit, but Romario ordered 20 mm. What should he do?
o: Have the supplier correct it now, before it is sent
Accept it, as 25 mm conduit will hold the wires more easily
Wait for the delivery and send back the wrong conduit then
Change his drawing to 25 mm so it matches the supplier
questions.why: The confirmation is checked so mistakes are caught before the goods leave the supplier. Correcting it now, and confirming in writing, saves a wrong delivery, a return trip and a delay.

questions.q: What should the bin card balance be after Thursday's issue?
o: 3 packets
13 packets
19 packets
23 packets
questions.why: 18 − 4 = 14, 14 − 5 = 9, 9 + 10 = 19, and 19 − 6 = 13. Forgetting Wednesday's delivery gives 3; stopping before Thursday gives 19.

questions.q: At what balance should Mrs Clarke reorder these electrodes?
o: 12 packets
20 packets
7 packets
17 packets
questions.why: Reorder level = usage per day × lead time + buffer stock = 3 × 4 + 5 = 17. The 12 packets used while waiting for delivery leave the 5-packet buffer untouched.

questions.q: Ten new packets arrive on Wednesday. Where should Nadine put them on the shelf?
o: In front of the old packets, where they are easiest to reach
Behind the older packets, so the older ones are issued first
On the floor beside the shelf until the old ones are used
In a separate cupboard, for the instructors only
questions.why: Putting new stock behind the old is how first in, first out works on the shelf. Older packets are issued before they can pick up damp or spoil, and nothing is left on the floor.

questions.q: At the end-of-term stocktake Nadine counts 11 packets, but the bin card shows 13. What should she do?
o: Count again, then report the difference to Mrs Clarke
Change the card to 11 and say nothing
Leave the card at 13, as the card is the official record
Take 2 packets from another store to make up the count
questions.why: A difference may be a counting slip, an unrecorded issue, damage or theft. Recount first, then report it, so the cause is found and the card is corrected with approval and a note of why.

questions.q: The driver wants Sheldon to sign straight away. What should Sheldon do?
o: Sign now and check the goods tomorrow morning
Refuse the whole delivery and send the truck back
Sign, as the driver is responsible for the goods
Check first, then sign with the problems noted
questions.why: A signature says the goods arrived complete and in good condition, so it comes after the check. Problems written on the note before signing are the evidence the supplier needs.

questions.q: What should Sheldon write on the delivery note about the flat bar?
o: 40 × 5 mm received; 40 × 6 mm ordered
Flat bar not quite right, to be checked
Flat bar received in poor condition
6 lengths of flat bar received, all OK
questions.why: A clear note gives exactly what arrived against what was ordered, so the supplier can put it right without argument. A vague note, or "OK", gives the supplier nothing to act on.

questions.q: What should Sheldon do with the 2 bent lengths of angle?
o: Straighten them in the press and use them in the trusses
Keep them apart, labelled and photographed
Put them in the scrap bin so nobody uses them by mistake
Cut them into short pieces for brackets and say nothing
questions.why: Damaged goods are kept separate, labelled and photographed until the supplier collects them or gives a credit note. Using or scrapping them loses the evidence, and bent steel may not be sound in a roof truss.

questions.q: A week later the supplier's invoice charges for 4 sheets of plate. What should the office do before paying?
o: Pay it, since the purchase order was for 4 sheets
Pay it and ask for the fourth sheet to be sent later
Match it with the PO and GRN, and query it
Refuse to pay any of it until the supplier phones them
questions.why: The invoice is matched with the purchase order and the goods received note before payment. The GRN shows only 3 sheets arrived, so the business asks for a credit note or the missing sheet.

questions.q: Which supplier gives Damion the best value for this job?
o: The welder's friend, as his price is the lowest
Supplier B, because its goods price is lower than A's
Supplier A, at the lowest total and in time for the job
Split it, buying the discs from B and the electrodes from A
questions.why: B's total with delivery is J$42,000, more than A's J$41,000, and B delivers after the job starts. A is approved, cheapest in total and on time, which is what best value means.

questions.q: What is wrong with buying from the welder's friend?
o: Nothing, if Damion pays from the petty cash
The seller is unapproved and the discs are unmarked
His price is too low, so the shop would pay too little GCT
Nothing, as long as the discs fit the grinders
questions.why: Approved suppliers have been checked for quality and fair dealing, and a receipt is needed for the records. An unmarked disc has no speed rating, so nobody can tell whether it is safe on the shop's grinders.

questions.q: Not every quote says whether GCT is included. What should Damion do?
o: Ask each supplier, then compare like with like
Assume the cheapest quote already includes GCT
Leave GCT out, as it is the same for every supplier
Add a guessed amount to the quotes that do not say
questions.why: A price with GCT cannot be compared fairly with one without it. Damion finds out what each price includes and compares them all the same way, at the current GCT rate.

questions.q: Damion has chosen his supplier. What is his next step?
o: Phone the supplier and order, then tell his supervisor next week
Ask the supplier to send its invoice so it can be paid first
Pay for the goods in cash and claim the money back later
Complete a purchase requisition for his supervisor to approve
questions.why: Spending is approved before the order is placed, so a requisition goes to the authorised person. After approval a signed purchase order is sent to the supplier.
